## IPBES map guideline tutorial

This is a walk-through tutorial on how to create maps using different sources of public data in accordance with the IPBES Technical Guidelines. Please note that to ensure all maps load correctly in the markdown file, run full code chunks rather than single code (in a script, the maps will load when running single lines of code).

First, load the libraries and data needed.

```{r libraries and data, include = FALSE}
# Set working directory to current file location
wd <- setwd(getwd())
message("Working directory set to: ", getwd())  

# Install relevant packages from renv.lock file
if (!require("renv")) install.packages("renv")
library(renv)
renv::restore(project = wd, prompt = F)

# Tool libraries
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)
library(countrycode)
library(httr)
library(envirem)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggspatial)

# Data libraries
library(geodata)
library(FAOSTAT)
library(rnaturalearth)
```

## Projections

A geographical projection is a representation of the world in a 2-dimensional space. This can be done in many different mathematical ways. The projection most recently recommended by the United Nations General Assembly (as of 04/09/2026) is the Equal Earth Projection since it best represents the true geographic size of the world's regions.

```{r projection}
# Define the projection using PROJ.4 notation
crs <- "+proj=eqearth +lon_0=0 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"
```

## Raster data

Raster data is represented as pixels that together form a grid. Continuous data can be well represented in raster format.

```{r plot raster data, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# Load January precipitation data from world clim
prec <- geodata::worldclim_global(var = "prec", res = 10, path = "data")[[1]]
terra::crs(prec) # world clim data uses unprojected coordinate system


# Ensure NAs are converted into correct format
jp <- prec * 1 


# Project world clim data onto Equal Earth
eqearth <- terra::project(jp, crs, mask=TRUE)


# Creates latitude and longitude labels and graticules (=latitutude and longitude lines)
lat <- c(-90, -60, -30, 0, 30, 60, 90)
long <- c(-180, -120, -60, 0, 60, 120, 180)
lines <- terra::graticule(lon = long, lat = lat, crs = crs)


# Plot graticules and precipitation data
plot(lines, lty = 5, col = "grey", retro=T) # plot graticules 
plot(eqearth, axes = F, col = rev(terrain.colors(255)), add = TRUE) # plot the raster
```

## Vector data

Vector data is represented by points, lines, or polygons/areas. Vector data is useful to portray boundaries or discrete data on a map. Here, coast lines are used to demonstrate what vector data looks like.

```{r plot vector data}
# Download land boundaries
coast <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 50, type = 'coastline', category = 'physical', returnclass = "sf")
coast <- coast %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = crs) # another way of projecting onto the Equal Earth format

# Plot regions
par(mar = c(0,0,0,0)) # set frame size
plot(lines, lty = 5, col = "grey", retro=T)
plot(coast, col="black", add = TRUE) 
```

## Combining Raster and Vector Data

It can be useful to combine the two data types. Plotting them on top of each other reveals how precipitation differs between continents.

```{r plot raster and vector data, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
par(mar = c(0,0,0,0))
plot(lines, lty = 5, col = "grey", retro=T)
plot(eqearth, axes = F, col = rev(terrain.colors(255)), add = TRUE)
plot(coast, col="black", add = TRUE) 
```

## Further layers

Loads of layers can be added onto a map. Below are some common ones that may be useful. Please note that country borders should not be included in IPBES maps.

```{r plotting several vector layers}
# Download ocean shapes and project onto Equal Earth
ocean <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 50, type = 'ocean', category = 'physical', returnclass = "sf")
ocean <- ocean %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = crs)
ocean <- ocean[,1]


# Download land boundaries
land <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 50, type = 'land', category = 'physical', returnclass = "sf")
land <- land %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = crs)


# Download major lakes
lakes <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 50, type = 'lakes', category = 'physical', returnclass = "sf")
lakes <- lakes %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = crs)


# Plot new layers
par(mar = c(0,0,0,0)) # set frame size
plot(lines, lty = 5, col = "grey", retro=T)
plot(ocean, col = alpha("lightskyblue", 0.3), add = TRUE)
plot(land, col = "white", add = TRUE)
plot(lakes, col = "lightblue", add = TRUE)
box(which = "plot", lty = "solid") # create figure frame
```

## How to handle country-level data

Since plotting country borders should be avoided in all IPBES reports, it is important to know how to aggregate country-level data by regions. Find an example on how to do this with the example of using continents as regions below.

```{r handling country level data, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
# Download population data from the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations; first register at https://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#developer-portal
#FAOSTAT::faostat_login(username = "yourusername", password = "yourpassword") # use your own credentials
#FAOSTAT::download_faostat_bulk("http://fenixservices.fao.org/faostat/static/bulkdownloads/Population_E_All_Data_(Normalized).zip", getwd())


# Load the data
pop_raw <- FAOSTAT::read_faostat_bulk("Population_E_All_Data_(Normalized).zip")


# Download countries shapefile
countries <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = 50, returnclass = "sf")
countries <- countries %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = crs)


# Clean the data to contain both sexes data from 2018
pop_2018 <- pop_raw %>% 
  dplyr::filter(element == "total_population___both_sexes" &
                  year == 2018) %>% 
  dplyr::select(area_code,
                area,
                element,
                year,
                unit,
                value)
tail(pop_2018$area, 35)

# When looking at the tail of the pop_2018 dataset, the last 34 rows are not country-level but pre-aggregated data. Since these do not reflect the regions of interest, they should be removed.
pop_2018 <- pop_2018[1:234, ] # Selects the first 234 records, thus removing the last 34 which are aggregated data

# To ensure continuity between the UN and Zenodo data regarding country naming conventions, ISO3 codes should be used instead of common country names 
pop_2018$ISO3_CODE <- countrycode(pop_2018$area, origin = "country.name", destination = "iso3c")

# check for anything that didn't match
print(pop_2018[is.na(pop_2018$ISO3_CODE), c("area", "ISO3_CODE")])

# assign missing ISO3 codes manually, find the codes here: https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/#search
pop_2018[57,7] <- "CUW" # Curaçao
pop_2018[173,7] <- "REU" # Réunion
pop_2018[177,7] <- "BLM" # Saint-Barthélemy
pop_2018[214,7] <- "TUR" # Türkiye
pop_2018 <- na.omit(pop_2018) # removes possible NAs

# Now join the continents onto our pop_2018 data
names(countries)[names(countries) == "iso_a3"] <- "ISO3_CODE" # rename column holding ISO3 codes

continents <-  countries %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% # drops the spatial attributes
  dplyr::select(ISO3_CODE, continent)  # filters the columns

pop_2018 <- dplyr::left_join(x = pop_2018, y = continents, by = "ISO3_CODE") %>% # joins data
  tidyr::drop_na() 


# Now, aggregate the data by continents
pop_2018 <- pop_2018 %>% 
  dplyr::group_by(continent) %>% # Grouping by continents
  dplyr::mutate(continent_pop = sum(value)/1000) %>% # calculates total population (millions) per continent
  dplyr::ungroup()


# Prepare data for mapping
data <- dplyr::full_join(x = countries, y = pop_2018, by = "ISO3_CODE") # to have geo data in same dataframe as regions

data_continent <- data %>% # this dissolves the data by region
  dplyr::group_by(continent.x) %>% 
  dplyr::summarise(continent_pop = sum(value, na.rm = T)/1000) 

data_continent$continent_pop <- round(data_continent$continent_pop) # round population numbers to full numbers


# Plotting by continents
par(mar = c(0,0,0,0))
plot(lines, lty = 5, col = "lightgrey",  retro=T)
plot(ocean, col = ggplot2::alpha("slategray1", 0.3), add = TRUE) 
plot(data_continent[,2], breaks = "quantile", add = TRUE)
box(which = "plot", lty = "solid")

# create unique categories and legend
palette <- hcl.colors(8, "Reds 3", rev = T) # colours

par(mar = c(0,0,0,0))
plot(lines, lty = 5, col = "lightgrey",  retro=T)
plot(ocean, col = ggplot2::alpha("slategray1", 0.3), add = TRUE) 
plot(data_continent[,2], pal = palette, add = TRUE)
legend("bottom", # adding the legend last 
       legend = (data_continent %>% pull(continent_pop) %>% sort()),
       fill = palette, 
       horiz = TRUE, bty = "n")
box(which = "plot", lty = "solid")
```

## Using ggplot for maps

Most people working in R are familiar with the plotting package ggplot2. Therefore, it is useful to know how to make maps with ggplot2 as well. Specialised packages like terra are better to use for official use as they were specifically designed to handle complex projections and map layouts. But for smaller, quickly produced maps e.g. for data exploration, ggplot2 can work just fine:

```{r map creation with ggplot2}
land <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 50, type = 'land', category = 'physical', returnclass = "sf")

# Map of region around Mexico
ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = land, color = "black", fill = "white") + # plots the land polygons
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-117.5, -86.5), ylim = c(14.5, 33.0)) + # sets the maps extent
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = gray(.5), # sets latitude and longitude lines 
        linetype = "dashed", size = 0.5),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#b3e5fc"), # sets background panel color 
        panel.border = element_rect(colour = "black", fill=NA, size=0.5))
```

Note: when plotting smaller regions (anything other than a world map) different projections might become appropriate to accurately and nicely reflect the scale of the region on the map. https://projectionwizard.org/ provides a good resource to understand at what scale which projections might be appropriate. It is recommended to research, which projection is best for the specific region and use of a smaller-scale map. https://spatialreference.org/ provides EPSG codes for a vast list of projections.


## IPBES regions

If IPBES regions should be plotted, they can be downloaded here (the shapefile is 500MB so this may take a few minutes):

```{r IPBES regions}
# Download IPBES regions and subregions data from Zenodo
recordID <- "3923633"
url_record <- paste0("https://zenodo.org/api/records/", recordID)
record <- httr::GET(url_record)
record # Status 200 indicates a successful download
View(content(record))


# Download the regions and subregions shapefile
url_shape <- content(record)$files[[1]]$links$self # retrieves the link
httr::GET(url_shape, write_disk("ipbes_regions_subregions.zip", overwrite = T))
unzip("ipbes_regions_subregions.zip") # unzips shapefile
shape <- sf::st_read("IPBES_Regions_Subregions2.shp") %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = crs)
```
